claim: Acvr1c mRNA (encoding ALK7) is expressed in interscapular BAT (iBAT) of young adult male mice at levels comparable to those found in inguinal WAT (iWAT).
source: Expression of Acvr1c mRNA (encoding ALK7) was detected in interscapular BAT (iBAT) of young adult male mice at levels comparable to those found in inguinal WAT (iWAT), although lower than Acvr1c mRNA expression in epididymal WAT (eWAT) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 1A showing relative Acvr1c mRNA expression levels across different tissues.

claim: Acvr1c mRNA expression in BAT is lower than in epididymal WAT (eWAT).
source: Expression of Acvr1c mRNA (encoding ALK7) was detected in interscapular BAT (iBAT) of young adult male mice at levels comparable to those found in inguinal WAT (iWAT), although lower than Acvr1c mRNA expression in epididymal WAT (eWAT) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 1A showing relative Acvr1c mRNA expression levels across different tissues.

claim: No Acvr1c mRNA expression could be detected in liver.
source: No Acvr1c mRNA expression could be detected in liver.
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 1A showing Acvr1c mRNA expression levels across different tissues.

claim: Acvr1c mRNA expression is low in cells isolated from BAT stromal vascular fraction (SVF).
source: The level of Acvr1c mRNA was low in cells isolated from BAT stromal vascular fraction (SVF), containing precursors of brown adipocytes, but was markedly upregulated after in vitro differentiation into brown adipocytes, reaching levels comparable to those found in mature adipocytes freshly isolated from BAT (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 1B showing Acvr1c mRNA expression in SVF cells, differentiated adipocytes, and mature adipocytes.

claim: Acvr1c mRNA expression is markedly upregulated after in vitro differentiation of BAT SVF cells into brown adipocytes.
source: The level of Acvr1c mRNA was low in cells isolated from BAT stromal vascular fraction (SVF), containing precursors of brown adipocytes, but was markedly upregulated after in vitro differentiation into brown adipocytes, reaching levels comparable to those found in mature adipocytes freshly isolated from BAT (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 1B showing Acvr1c mRNA expression in SVF cells, differentiated adipocytes, and mature adipocytes.

claim: Acvr1c mRNA expression in differentiated brown adipocytes reaches levels comparable to those found in mature adipocytes freshly isolated from BAT.
source: The level of Acvr1c mRNA was low in cells isolated from BAT stromal vascular fraction (SVF), containing precursors of brown adipocytes, but was markedly upregulated after in vitro differentiation into brown adipocytes, reaching levels comparable to those found in mature adipocytes freshly isolated from BAT (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 1B showing Acvr1c mRNA expression in SVF cells, differentiated adipocytes, and mature adipocytes.

claim: Acvr1c mRNA expression in BAT was almost completely abolished in Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutant mice.
source: In the resulting mutant mice (Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx), Acvr1c mRNA expression in BAT was almost completely abolished (Figure 1C), confirming that ALK7 is exclusively expressed by brown adipocytes in this tissue.
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 1C showing Acvr1c mRNA expression in BAT of mutant and control mice.

claim: ALK7 is exclusively expressed by brown adipocytes in BAT.
source: In the resulting mutant mice (Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx), Acvr1c mRNA expression in BAT was almost completely abolished (Figure 1C), confirming that ALK7 is exclusively expressed by brown adipocytes in this tissue.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Ucp1-CRE driven deletion of Alk7 in brown adipocytes results in almost complete loss of Acvr1c mRNA in BAT.

claim: Acvr1c expression was spared in hypothalamus of Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutant mice.
source: Acvr1c expression was spared in other tissues, including hypothalamus (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 1C showing Acvr1c mRNA expression in hypothalamus of mutant and control mice.

claim: At 2 months of age, Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutant mice showed body weight indistinguishable from control mice under Chow diet.
source: At 2 months of age, Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutant mice showed body weight and fat composition indistinguishable from control mice under Chow diet (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight measurements presented in Figure 1D.

claim: At 2 months of age, Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutant mice showed fat composition indistinguishable from control mice under Chow diet.
source: At 2 months of age, Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutant mice showed body weight and fat composition indistinguishable from control mice under Chow diet (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fat and lean mass measurements presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Energy consumption was not affected by the lack of ALK7 in BAT, as demonstrated by normal oxygen consumption (VO2) under both fed and fasted conditions.
source: Energy consumption was not affected by the lack of ALK7 in BAT, as demonstrated by normal oxygen consumption (VO2) under both fed and fasted conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by indirect calorimetry data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing VO2 measurements.

claim: Respiratory exchange ratio (RER) was comparable between Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx and control mice.
source: Similarly, respiratory exchange ratio (RER), which reports the relative usage of carbohydrates and fat, and food intake were also comparable between Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx and control mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by indirect calorimetry data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing RER measurements.

claim: Food intake was comparable between Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx and control mice.
source: Similarly, respiratory exchange ratio (RER), which reports the relative usage of carbohydrates and fat, and food intake were also comparable between Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx and control mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by food consumption data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both iBAT and eWAT mass relative to body weight were normal in 2 month old Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutants.
source: Both iBAT and eWAT mass relative to body weight were also normal in 2 month old mutants (Figure 1E), as well as expression of a battery of BAT differentiation and maturation markers and mitochondrial copy number (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B), indicating that ALK7 is not required by brown adipocytes for normal BAT development.
evidence: The claim is supported by tissue mass measurements presented in Figure 1E.

claim: Expression of BAT differentiation and maturation markers was normal in 2 month old Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutants.
source: Both iBAT and eWAT mass relative to body weight were also normal in 2 month old mutants (Figure 1E), as well as expression of a battery of BAT differentiation and maturation markers and mitochondrial copy number (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B), indicating that ALK7 is not required by brown adipocytes for normal BAT development.
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A showing mRNA expression of differentiation and maturation markers.

claim: Mitochondrial copy number was normal in 2 month old Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutants.
source: Both iBAT and eWAT mass relative to body weight were also normal in 2 month old mutants (Figure 1E), as well as expression of a battery of BAT differentiation and maturation markers and mitochondrial copy number (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B), indicating that ALK7 is not required by brown adipocytes for normal BAT development.
evidence: The claim is supported by mitochondrial DNA content data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: ALK7 is not required by brown adipocytes for normal BAT development.
source: Both iBAT and eWAT mass relative to body weight were also normal in 2 month old mutants (Figure 1E), as well as expression of a battery of BAT differentiation and maturation markers and mitochondrial copy number (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B), indicating that ALK7 is not required by brown adipocytes for normal BAT development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that multiple markers of BAT development and function are normal in mutant mice lacking ALK7 in brown adipocytes.

claim: Overnight (14 hr) fasting induced a significant reduction in iBAT weight in 2 month old Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mice.
source: Interestingly, overnight (14 hr) fasting induced a significant reduction in iBAT weight in 2 month old Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mice, despite normal eWAT mass (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by tissue mass measurements after fasting presented in Figure 1F.

claim: eWAT mass was normal in 2 month old Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mice after overnight fasting.
source: Interestingly, overnight (14 hr) fasting induced a significant reduction in iBAT weight in 2 month old Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mice, despite normal eWAT mass (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by tissue mass measurements after fasting presented in Figure 1F.

claim: Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutant mice showed a significant decrease in lipid droplet size in iBAT compared to age-matched controls.
source: Histological analysis of iBAT revealed a significant decrease in lipid droplet size in 2 month old Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mice compared to age-matched controls (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by BODIPY staining and quantitative analysis of lipid droplet size presented in Figure 2A.

claim: A similar reduction in lipid droplet size was observed in the iBAT of global Alk7-/- knock-out mice.
source: A similar reduction was observed in the iBAT of global Alk7-/- knock-out mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by BODIPY staining and quantitative analysis of lipid droplet size presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A proteomics analysis of iBAT lipid droplets from Alk7-/- knock-out mice revealed increased levels of adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL).
source: A proteomics analysis of iBAT lipid droplets from Alk7-/- knock-out mice revealed increased levels of adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL), the rate-limiting enzyme of lipolysis, despite normal levels of other major lipid droplet proteins, including hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic analysis data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: ATGL is the rate-limiting enzyme of lipolysis.
source: A proteomics analysis of iBAT lipid droplets from Alk7-/- knock-out mice revealed increased levels of adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL), the rate-limiting enzyme of lipolysis, despite normal levels of other major lipid droplet proteins, including hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the context of describing ATGL.

claim: Levels of other major lipid droplet proteins, including hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL), were normal in iBAT lipid droplets from Alk7-/- knock-out mice.
source: A proteomics analysis of iBAT lipid droplets from Alk7-/- knock-out mice revealed increased levels of adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL), the rate-limiting enzyme of lipolysis, despite normal levels of other major lipid droplet proteins, including hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic analysis data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Total iBAT lysates from Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx conditional mutant mice showed increased ATGL levels compared to controls, although the difference did not reach statistical significance (p=0.077).
source: Total iBAT lysates from Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx conditional mutant mice showed increased ATGL levels compared to controls (Figure 2C), although the difference did not reach statistical significance (p=0.077).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis presented in Figure 2C.

claim: ATGL protein levels were robustly increased in the mutant iBAT 14 hr after fasting.
source: However, ATGL protein levels were robustly increased in the mutant iBAT 14 hr after fasting (Figure 2C), which was in line with the reduced iBAT mass observed in fasted mutant animals (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis presented in Figure 2C.

claim: ATGL levels were not changed by fasting in BAT of wild type mice.
source: ATGL levels were not changed by fasting in BAT of wild type mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No differences could be detected in the levels of phosphorylated HSL (P-HSLS563) between Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutant and control mice.
source: No differences could be detected in the levels of phosphorylated HSL (P-HSLS563, Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis presented in Figure 2C.

claim: mRNA levels of Adrb1 and Adrb3 were not significantly different between genotypes in either fed or fasted conditions.
source: In agreement with this, mRNA levels of Adrb1 and Adrb3, encoding catecholamine receptors in adipocytes, were not significantly different between genotypes in either fed or fasted conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Enhanced ATGL protein levels in the mutants were accompanied by a strong trend (p=0.078) towards increased Atgl mRNA levels after fasting.
source: Enhanced ATGL protein levels in the mutants were accompanied by a strong trend (p=0.078) towards increased Atgl mRNA levels after fasting (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: iBAT from fasted conditional mutant mice showed a significant decrease in the mRNA levels of G0/G1 switch gene 2 (G0S2).
source: iBAT from fasted conditional mutant mice also showed a significant decrease in the mRNA levels of G0/G1 switch gene 2 (G0S2), which encodes an inhibitor of ATGL activity (Yang et al., 2010; Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 2E.

claim: G0S2 encodes an inhibitor of ATGL activity.
source: iBAT from fasted conditional mutant mice also showed a significant decrease in the mRNA levels of G0/G1 switch gene 2 (G0S2), which encodes an inhibitor of ATGL activity (Yang et al., 2010; Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2010.

claim: Elevated levels of C/EBPα were found in iBAT from fasted conditional mutant mice.
source: In addition, we found elevated levels of C/EBPα (Figure 2F), a well known regulator of adipocyte differentiation which has been shown to collaborate with PPARγ to upregulate ATGL expression in adipocytes (Yogosawa et al., 2013; Hasan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis presented in Figure 2F.

claim: C/EBPα is a well known regulator of adipocyte differentiation.
source: In addition, we found elevated levels of C/EBPα (Figure 2F), a well known regulator of adipocyte differentiation which has been shown to collaborate with PPARγ to upregulate ATGL expression in adipocytes (Yogosawa et al., 2013; Hasan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge.

claim: C/EBPα has been shown to collaborate with PPARγ to upregulate ATGL expression in adipocytes.
source: In addition, we found elevated levels of C/EBPα (Figure 2F), a well known regulator of adipocyte differentiation which has been shown to collaborate with PPARγ to upregulate ATGL expression in adipocytes (Yogosawa et al., 2013; Hasan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yogosawa et al., 2013 and Hasan et al., 2018.

claim: Significantly increased levels of glycerol were detected in explant supernatants derived from fasted mutant mice compared to controls.
source: Significantly increased levels of glycerol were detected in explant supernatants derived from fasted mutant mice compared to controls (Figure 2G), indicating abnormally enhanced basal lipolysis in iBAT of Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mice after fasting.
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo lipolysis assay data presented in Figure 2G.

claim: Increased glycerol levels in explant supernatants indicate abnormally enhanced basal lipolysis in iBAT of Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mice after fasting.
source: Significantly increased levels of glycerol were detected in explant supernatants derived from fasted mutant mice compared to controls (Figure 2G), indicating abnormally enhanced basal lipolysis in iBAT of Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mice after fasting.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that glycerol release, a marker of lipolysis, is increased in mutant BAT explants.

claim: Basal levels of AKT phosphorylated on Ser473 (P-AKTS473) were unchanged in iBAT of conditional mutant mice relative to controls, both under fed or fasted conditions.
source: Basal levels of AKT, a key downstream effector of insulin signaling, phosphorylated on Ser473 (P-AKTS473), which correlates with its activation state, were unchanged in iBAT of conditional mutant mice relative to controls, both under fed or fasted conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: P-AKTS473 levels were not changed by fasting in iBAT of wild type mice.
source: P-AKTS473 levels were neither changed by fasting in iBAT of wild type mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: P-AKTS473 levels were increased to the same extent in iBAT of both mutant and control mice in response to acute insulin administration.
source: In addition, P-AKTS473 levels were increased to the same extent in iBAT of both mutant and control mice in response to acute insulin administration (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), indicating normal insulin sensitivity in iBAT lacking ALK7.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: iBAT lacking ALK7 has normal insulin sensitivity.
source: In addition, P-AKTS473 levels were increased to the same extent in iBAT of both mutant and control mice in response to acute insulin administration (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), indicating normal insulin sensitivity in iBAT lacking ALK7.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that insulin-induced AKT phosphorylation is normal in mutant BAT.

claim: A microarray analysis of iBAT from Alk7-/- global knock-out mice revealed several changes in gene expression in mutant iBAT compared to wild type controls.
source: A microarray analysis of iBAT from Alk7-/- global knock-out mice revealed several changes in gene expression in mutant iBAT compared to wild type controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), including upregulation in the level of Prodh mRNA, encoding proline dehydrogenase (POX), a mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the first step in the degradation of proline, and a critical component of metabolic responses to nutrient stress in cancer cells (Pandhare et al., 2009; Phang, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Prodh mRNA, encoding proline dehydrogenase (POX), was upregulated in iBAT from Alk7-/- global knock-out mice.
source: A microarray analysis of iBAT from Alk7-/- global knock-out mice revealed several changes in gene expression in mutant iBAT compared to wild type controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), including upregulation in the level of Prodh mRNA, encoding proline dehydrogenase (POX), a mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the first step in the degradation of proline, and a critical component of metabolic responses to nutrient stress in cancer cells (Pandhare et al., 2009; Phang, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: POX is a mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the first step in the degradation of proline.
source: A microarray analysis of iBAT from Alk7-/- global knock-out mice revealed several changes in gene expression in mutant iBAT compared to wild type controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), including upregulation in the level of Prodh mRNA, encoding proline dehydrogenase (POX), a mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the first step in the degradation of proline, and a critical component of metabolic responses to nutrient stress in cancer cells (Pandhare et al., 2009; Phang, 2019).
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge.

claim: POX is a critical component of metabolic responses to nutrient stress in cancer cells.
source: A microarray analysis of iBAT from Alk7-/- global knock-out mice revealed several changes in gene expression in mutant iBAT compared to wild type controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), including upregulation in the level of Prodh mRNA, encoding proline dehydrogenase (POX), a mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the first step in the degradation of proline, and a critical component of metabolic responses to nutrient stress in cancer cells (Pandhare et al., 2009; Phang, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pandhare et al., 2009 and Phang, 2019.

claim: Prodh mRNA levels were increased after 14 hr fasting in iBAT of both Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx conditional mutant and control mice, but significantly more so in the mutants.
source: In line with this, Prodh mRNA levels were increased after 14 hr fasting in iBAT of both Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx conditional mutant and control mice, but significantly more so in the mutants (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: mRNAs encoding enzymes involved in the degradation of alanine and branched amino acids, namely ALT1 and BCAT2, were specifically upregulated upon fasting in the mutant iBAT.
source: Similarly, mRNAs encoding enzymes involved in the degradation of alanine and branched amino acids, namely ALT1 and BCAT2, were also specifically upregulated upon fasting in the mutant iBAT (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Prodh, Alt1, and Bcat2 genes are all targets of KLF15.
source: Realizing that these three genes are all targets of KLF15, a key regulator of responses to nutritional stress in liver and skeletal muscle (Gray et al., 2007; Haldar et al., 2012), we examined the levels of Klf15 mRNA in mutant and control iBAT.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gray et al., 2007 and Haldar et al., 2012.

claim: KLF15 is a key regulator of responses to nutritional stress in liver and skeletal muscle.
source: Realizing that these three genes are all targets of KLF15, a key regulator of responses to nutritional stress in liver and skeletal muscle (Gray et al., 2007; Haldar et al., 2012), we examined the levels of Klf15 mRNA in mutant and control iBAT.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gray et al., 2007 and Haldar et al., 2012.

claim: A significant induction of Klf15 mRNA after fasting was observed in iBAT from Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutant mice, but not from control mice.
source: This revealed a significant induction of Klf15 mRNA after fasting in iBAT from Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutant mice, but not from control mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Fasting induced Klf15 mRNA in the liver regardless of genotype.
source: As expected, fasting induced Klf15 mRNA in the liver regardless of genotype (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: At the protein level, similar changes were observed for KLF15, ALT1, BCAT2 and POX, with fasting inducing a more pronounced increase in mutant BAT compared to control.
source: At the protein level, similar changes were observed for KLF15 (Figure 3D), ALT1, BCAT2 (Figure 3E) and POX (see below). In all cases, fasting induced a more pronounced increase in mutant BAT compared to control.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis presented in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: Klf15 is one major target of glucocorticoid signaling, mediating several catabolic responses to glucocorticoids in liver and skeletal muscle.
source: Klf15 is one major target of glucocorticoid signaling, mediating several catabolic responses to glucocorticoids in liver and skeletal muscle (Shimizu et al., 2011; Sasse et al., 2013), but its role and regulation in BAT had not been investigated.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Shimizu et al., 2011 and Sasse et al., 2013.

claim: The role and regulation of Klf15 in BAT had not been investigated.
source: Klf15 is one major target of glucocorticoid signaling, mediating several catabolic responses to glucocorticoids in liver and skeletal muscle (Shimizu et al., 2011; Sasse et al., 2013), but its role and regulation in BAT had not been investigated.
evidence: The claim is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: Overnight fasting increased corticosterone levels in serum of both Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutants and control mice to a similar extent.
source: We first verified that overnight fasting increased corticosterone levels in serum of both Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutants and control mice to a similar extent (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by serum corticosterone measurements presented in Figure 3F.

claim: Klf15 mRNA levels were reduced by RU486 treatment in both strains of mice.
source: Klf15 mRNA levels were reduced by RU486 treatment in both strains of mice (Figure 3G), indicating that Klf15 expression is also under glucocorticoid regulation in BAT.
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 3G.

claim: Klf15 expression is under glucocorticoid regulation in BAT.
source: Klf15 mRNA levels were reduced by RU486 treatment in both strains of mice (Figure 3G), indicating that Klf15 expression is also under glucocorticoid regulation in BAT.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the glucocorticoid receptor antagonist RU486 reduces Klf15 mRNA levels in BAT.

claim: RU486 treatment restored Prodh mRNA levels in iBAT of conditional mutant mice back to the level found in control mice.
source: Importantly, RU486 treatment also restored Prodh mRNA levels in iBAT of conditional mutant mice back to the level found in control mice (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 3H.

claim: Expression of Alt1 and Bcat2 mRNAs were not affected by RU486 treatment.
source: Expression of Alt1 and Bcat2 mRNAs were not affected by RU486 treatment (Figure 3I,J), suggesting perhaps a lower sensitivity to KLF15 levels in these genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figures 3I and 3J.

claim: Alt1 and Bcat2 genes may have lower sensitivity to KLF15 levels.
source: Expression of Alt1 and Bcat2 mRNAs were not affected by RU486 treatment (Figure 3I,J), suggesting perhaps a lower sensitivity to KLF15 levels in these genes.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on the observation that RU486 treatment does not affect Alt1 and Bcat2 mRNA levels despite reducing Klf15 levels.

claim: After 10 days of differentiation, the expression of mRNAs for Klf15, Prodh, Alt1 and Bcat2 were strongly upregulated in brown adipocyte cultures compared to the levels in iBAT SVF cells.
source: After 10 days of differentiation, the expression of mRNAs for Klf15, Prodh, Alt1 and Bcat2 were strongly upregulated in these cultures compared to the levels in iBAT SVF cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: Treatment with the ALK7 ligand activin B significantly reduced the expression of Klf15, Prodh, Alt1 and Bcat2 mRNAs in differentiated brown adipocytes.
source: Treatment with the ALK7 ligand activin B significantly reduced the expression of the four mRNAs in differentiated brown adipocytes (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: The response to activin B was effectively suppressed by SB431542, an inhibitor of type I receptors for TGF-βs and activins, including ALK7.
source: This response was effectively suppressed by SB431542, an inhibitor of type I receptors for TGF-βs and activins, including ALK7 (Inman et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 4B and citation to Inman et al., 2002.

claim: SB431542 is an inhibitor of type I receptors for TGF-βs and activins, including ALK7.
source: This response was effectively suppressed by SB431542, an inhibitor of type I receptors for TGF-βs and activins, including ALK7 (Inman et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Inman et al., 2002.

claim: SB431542 could on its own moderately increase the mRNA expression of Klf15, Prodh, Alt1 and Bcat2, although the effect did not reach statistical significance.
source: Interestingly, SB431542 could on its own moderately increase the mRNA expression of the four genes, although the effect did not reach statistical significance (Figure 4B), perhaps reflecting the activities of endogenously produced ligands.
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: The effect of SB431542 on increasing mRNA expression may reflect the activities of endogenously produced ligands.
source: Interestingly, SB431542 could on its own moderately increase the mRNA expression of the four genes, although the effect did not reach statistical significance (Figure 4B), perhaps reflecting the activities of endogenously produced ligands.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on the observation that SB431542 alone can increase mRNA expression.

claim: Activin B had no effect on brown adipocytes lacking ALK7.
source: Activin B had no effect on brown adipocytes lacking ALK7 (Figure 4C), indicating that its effects were mediated by the ALK7 receptor.
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: The effects of activin B on brown adipocytes were mediated by the ALK7 receptor.
source: Activin B had no effect on brown adipocytes lacking ALK7 (Figure 4C), indicating that its effects were mediated by the ALK7 receptor.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that activin B has no effect in cells lacking ALK7.

claim: Treatment with activin B increased G0S2 mRNA expression in cultured brown adipocytes.
source: In line with the reduced G0S2 mRNA levels observed in iBAT from fasted Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutants (Figure 2F), treatment with activin B increased, while SB431542 decreased, expression of this gene in cultured brown adipocytes (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: SB431542 decreased G0S2 mRNA expression in cultured brown adipocytes.
source: In line with the reduced G0S2 mRNA levels observed in iBAT from fasted Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutants (Figure 2F), treatment with activin B increased, while SB431542 decreased, expression of this gene in cultured brown adipocytes (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: A trend towards reduction of Atgl mRNA expression with activin B was detected, but did not reach statistical significance.
source: We detected a trend towards reduction of Atgl mRNA expression with activin B, and increased expression with SB431542, in agreement with the results in vivo, but these trends did not reach statistical significance.
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: A trend towards increased Atgl mRNA expression with SB431542 was detected, but did not reach statistical significance.
source: We detected a trend towards reduction of Atgl mRNA expression with activin B, and increased expression with SB431542, in agreement with the results in vivo, but these trends did not reach statistical significance.
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: Regulation of Atgl mRNA expression by ALK7 may require additional, fasting-induced signals.
source: Regulation of Atgl mRNA expression by ALK7 may require additional, fasting-induced signals.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on the observation that activin B effects on Atgl mRNA are not statistically significant in vitro.

claim: Activin B had no significant effects on the mRNA levels of Ucp1 or Prdm16.
source: Activin B had not significant effects on the mRNA levels of Ucp1 or Prdm16 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In cultured human brown adipocytes, activin B treatment resulted in reduced levels of Klf15 and Prodh mRNAs.
source: Importantly, similar observations could be made in cultured human brown adipocytes, in which activin B treatment also resulted in reduced levels of Klf15 and Prodh mRNAs (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 4E.

claim: ALK7 signaling can directly suppress the expression of mRNAs encoding diverse regulators of fat and amino acid catabolism.
source: Together these results suggest that ALK7 signaling can directly suppress the expression of a series of mRNAs encoding diverse regulators of fat and amino acid catabolism.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that activin B treatment reduces expression of catabolic genes in cultured brown adipocytes.

claim: iBAT from mutant mice showed a moderate increase in POX protein levels compared to control mice.
source: iBAT from mutant mice showed a moderate increase in POX protein levels compared to control mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Fasting induced a significantly greater increase in POX protein levels in the mutant iBAT.
source: However, fasting induced a significantly greater increase in POX protein levels in the mutant iBAT (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis presented in Figure 5A.

claim: SDHA, a subunit of succinate dehydrogenase, was differentially enhanced by fasting in the mutant iBAT.
source: In addition, SDHA, a subunit of succinate dehydrogenase, was also differentially enhanced by fasting in the mutant iBAT (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis presented in Figure 5A.

claim: POX and succinate dehydrogenase are both physically and functionally coupled in mitochondrial complex II.
source: Interestingly, POX and succinate dehydrogenase are both physically and functionally coupled in mitochondrial complex II (Hancock et al., 2016).

claim: None of the other mitochondrial proteins investigated were found to be affected in the mutants, including UCP1, COXIV, Rieske FeS, NDUFA10 and beta F1 ATPase.

evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: Levels of POX and UCP1 were not significantly changed by fasting in BAT of wild type mice.
source: Levels of POX and UCP1 were not significantly changed by fasting in BAT of wild type mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Addition of proline to mitochondria isolated from iBAT of fasted mice failed to induce ROS production, regardless of genotype.
source: However, in our hands, addition of proline to mitochondria isolated from iBAT of fasted mice failed to induce ROS production, regardless of genotype (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROS production assay data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Proline supported a modest increase in ATP production in mitochondria isolated from BAT of fasted control mice.
source: Compared to its effects on liver mitochondria (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), proline supported a modest increase in ATP production in mitochondria isolated from BAT of fasted control mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP synthesis assay data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: ATP generation was significantly elevated in BAT mitochondria of fasted Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutant mice compared to controls.
source: However, ATP generation was significantly elevated in BAT mitochondria of fasted Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutant mice compared to controls (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP synthesis assay data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Nutrient stress induces elevated levels of POX which lead to enhanced ATP generation in mitochondria from BAT lacking ALK7.
source: These results suggest that nutrient stress induces elevated levels of POX which in turn lead to enhanced ATP generation in mitochondria from BAT lacking ALK7.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that fasted mutant BAT has increased POX levels and increased proline-dependent ATP generation.

claim: In fed mice, a 4 hr cold exposure did not reveal any alterations in VO2, body temperature, RER or activity in the mutant mice compared to controls.
source: In fed mice, a 4 hr cold exposure did not reveal any alterations in either VO2, body temperature, RER (Figure 6A to C) or activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) in the mutant mice compared to controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by indirect calorimetry and body temperature data presented in Figures 6A-C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mutant animals that had been fasted were unable to keep the higher levels of VO2 observed in control animals during cold exposure.
source: However, significant changes were observed in animals that had been fasted for 14 hr prior to cold exposure. Mutant animals that had been fasted were unable to keep the higher levels of VO2 observed in control animals (Figure 6D) and, as a consequence, displayed a very rapid drop in body temperature (Figure 6E), with over 70% of animals showing temperatures lower than 32°C after 3 hr (compared to 20% of controls).
evidence: The claim is supported by indirect calorimetry data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: Fasted mutant animals displayed a very rapid drop in body temperature during cold exposure.
source: However, significant changes were observed in animals that had been fasted for 14 hr prior to cold exposure. Mutant animals that had been fasted were unable to keep the higher levels of VO2 observed in control animals (Figure 6D) and, as a consequence, displayed a very rapid drop in body temperature (Figure 6E), with over 70% of animals showing temperatures lower than 32°C after 3 hr (compared to 20% of controls).
evidence: The claim is supported by body temperature measurements presented in Figure 6E.

claim: Over 70% of fasted mutant animals showed temperatures lower than 32°C after 3 hr of cold exposure (compared to 20% of controls).
source: However, significant changes were observed in animals that had been fasted for 14 hr prior to cold exposure. Mutant animals that had been fasted were unable to keep the higher levels of VO2 observed in control animals (Figure 6D) and, as a consequence, displayed a very rapid drop in body temperature (Figure 6E), with over 70% of animals showing temperatures lower than 32°C after 3 hr (compared to 20% of controls).
evidence: The claim is supported by body temperature measurements presented in Figure 6E.

claim: Overall activity was similar to controls in the mutant mice during cold exposure after fasting.
source: Overall activity was similar to controls in the mutant mice during this period (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by activity measurements presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both genotypes showed a similar switch to usage of free-fatty acids (FFA) as energy source during cold exposure after fasting, as shown by RER close to 0.7.
source: In these conditions, both genotypes showed a similar switch to usage of free-fatty acids (FFA) as energy source, as shown by RER close to 0.7 (Figure 6F), in line with the low levels of serum glucose and insulin observed upon cold exposure, which did not show differences between genotypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RER measurements presented in Figure 6F.

claim: Low levels of serum glucose and insulin were observed upon cold exposure after fasting, which did not show differences between genotypes.
source: In these conditions, both genotypes showed a similar switch to usage of free-fatty acids (FFA) as energy source, as shown by RER close to 0.7 (Figure 6F), in line with the low levels of serum glucose and insulin observed upon cold exposure, which did not show differences between genotypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by serum glucose and insulin measurements presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Both mutants and controls showed similar serum levels of FFA and triglycerides during cold exposure after fasting.
source: Both mutants and controls also showed similar serum levels of FFA and triglycerides (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E,F), indicating normal uptake of circulating lipids in the mutants (abnormal uptake is known to result in elevated levels in serum).
evidence: The claim is supported by serum FFA and triglyceride measurements presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Normal uptake of circulating lipids occurs in the mutants.
source: Both mutants and controls also showed similar serum levels of FFA and triglycerides (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E,F), indicating normal uptake of circulating lipids in the mutants (abnormal uptake is known to result in elevated levels in serum).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that serum lipid levels are normal in mutants.

claim: Mutant mice exposed to 5°C for 8 hr with unrestricted access to food showed no difference in body temperature compared to controls.
source: We note that mutant mice exposed to 5°C for 8 hr with unrestricted access to food showed no difference in body temperature compared to controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G), indicating that the deficit in the mutants is specific to situations of nutritional stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by body temperature measurements presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The deficit in the mutants is specific to situations of nutritional stress.
source: We note that mutant mice exposed to 5°C for 8 hr with unrestricted access to food showed no difference in body temperature compared to controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G), indicating that the deficit in the mutants is specific to situations of nutritional stress.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mutants only show temperature deficits when fasted, not when fed.

claim: NE content and turnover was comparable in iBAT from fasted mutant and control mice during cold exposure.
source: NE content and turnover was comparable in iBAT from fasted mutant and control mice during cold exposure (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by NE turnover measurements presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Ucp1 mRNA was similarly induced by cold exposure in both genotypes.
source: Also, Ucp1 mRNA was similarly induced by cold exposure in both genotypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), and levels of activated mTORC2 (phosphorylated at Ser2481) and HSL (phosphorylated at Ser563), which are targets of NE signaling in BAT (Albert et al., 2016), were similar in fasted mutant and control mice upon cold exposure (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C,D), suggesting normal NE signaling in mutant BAT.
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Levels of activated mTORC2 (phosphorylated at Ser2481) and HSL (phosphorylated at Ser563) were similar in fasted mutant and control mice upon cold exposure.
source: Also, Ucp1 mRNA was similarly induced by cold exposure in both genotypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), and levels of activated mTORC2 (phosphorylated at Ser2481) and HSL (phosphorylated at Ser563), which are targets of NE signaling in BAT (Albert et al., 2016), were similar in fasted mutant and control mice upon cold exposure (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C,D), suggesting normal NE signaling in mutant BAT.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: mTORC2 and HSL are targets of NE signaling in BAT.
source: Also, Ucp1 mRNA was similarly induced by cold exposure in both genotypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), and levels of activated mTORC2 (phosphorylated at Ser2481) and HSL (phosphorylated at Ser563), which are targets of NE signaling in BAT (Albert et al., 2016), were similar in fasted mutant and control mice upon cold exposure (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C,D), suggesting normal NE signaling in mutant BAT.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Albert et al., 2016.

claim: NE signaling is normal in mutant BAT.
source: Also, Ucp1 mRNA was similarly induced by cold exposure in both genotypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), and levels of activated mTORC2 (phosphorylated at Ser2481) and HSL (phosphorylated at Ser563), which are targets of NE signaling in BAT (Albert et al., 2016), were similar in fasted mutant and control mice upon cold exposure (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C,D), suggesting normal NE signaling in mutant BAT.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that NE-responsive markers are normal in mutant BAT.

claim: Hypothermia in mice lacking ALK7 in BAT may be the consequence of abnormally high catabolism of fat and amino acids upon nutrient stress, resulting in depletion of energy depots necessary to defend body temperature upon cold exposure.
source: Together, these results suggest that hypothermia in mice lacking ALK7 in BAT may be the consequence of abnormally high catabolism of fat and amino acids upon nutrient stress, resulting in depletion of energy depots necessary to defend body temperature upon cold exposure.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective observations of increased catabolic activity and hypothermia in fasted mutant mice.

claim: A significant drop in body temperature was observed in the mutants during the last week of chronic cold exposure at 10°C.
source: Control and mutant animals of matched age and weights were first cold adapted for 14 days at 18°C, and then placed at 10°C for 21 days. While control animals maintained body temperature throughout the experiment, a significant drop in body temperature was observed in the mutants during the last week of the treatment (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by body temperature measurements presented in Figure 6G.

claim: A decrease in relative iBAT weight was observed in the mutants exposed to chronic cold, but not in eWAT weight.
source: This was accompanied by a decrease in relative iBAT weight in the mutants exposed to cold, similar to that observed upon fasting, but not in eWAT weight (Figure 6H and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by tissue mass measurements presented in Figures 6H and I.

claim: Body weight and food intake were comparable in the two genotypes after chronic cold exposure.
source: Body weight and food intake were comparable in the two genotypes after cold exposure (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight and food intake measurements presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Ucp1 mRNA was induced to similar levels by prolonged cold treatment in BAT of control and mutant mice.
source: Also Ucp1 mRNA was induced to similar levels by prolonged cold treatment in BAT of control and mutant mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Several thermogenic markers were induced to comparable levels in iWAT of both genotypes after prolonged cold exposure.
source: We therefore examined expression of several thermogenic markers in iWAT of control and Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutant mice after prolonged cold exposure, but found that they were induced to comparable levels in both genotypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A–E), indicating normal browning of iWAT in conditional mutant mice after cold exposure.
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 4A–E.

claim: Browning of iWAT is normal in conditional mutant mice after cold exposure.
source: We therefore examined expression of several thermogenic markers in iWAT of control and Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutant mice after prolonged cold exposure, but found that they were induced to comparable levels in both genotypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A–E), indicating normal browning of iWAT in conditional mutant mice after cold exposure.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that thermogenic markers are induced normally in iWAT of mutant mice.

claim: Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutant mice are inadequately adapted to prolonged cold exposure, perhaps due to premature depletion of energy depots in BAT.
source: These results indicate that Ucp1CRE:Alk7fx/fx mutant mice are inadequately adapted to prolonged cold exposure, perhaps due to premature depletion of energy depots in BAT, even in conditions of unrestricted food access.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mutant mice show hypothermia and reduced BAT mass during chronic cold exposure.

claim: ALK7 functions to dampen catabolic activities triggered in BAT upon limited nutrient availability.
source: Based on the results of the present study, we propose that ALK7 functions to dampen catabolic activities triggered in BAT upon limited nutrient availability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective observations that loss of ALK7 leads to increased catabolic activity in BAT under nutrient stress.

claim: Under nutrient stress, catabolic functions become abnormally amplified in brown adipocytes lacking ALK7, leaving the tissue energetically unable to cope with the demands imposed by low ambient temperatures.
source: Under nutrient stress, these catabolic functions, for example lipolysis and amino acid degradation, become abnormally amplified in brown adipocytes lacking ALK7, leaving the tissue energetically unable to cope with the demands imposed by low ambient temperatures.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective observations of increased catabolic activity and hypothermia in fasted mutant mice exposed to cold.

claim: Circulating energy substrates are sufficient to fuel non-shivering thermogenesis under conditions that blunt BAT lipolysis, even upon acute cold exposure in the absence of food.
source: Recent studies have reported that circulating energy substrates are sufficient to fuel non-shivering thermogenesis under conditions that blunt BAT lipolysis, even upon acute cold exposure in the absence of food (Schreiber et al., 2017; Shin et al., 2017), leading to the notion that lipid droplet lipolysis in brown adipocytes is not essential for cold-induced thermogenesis regardless of food availability (Shin et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schreiber et al., 2017 and Shin et al., 2017.

claim: Energy reservoirs within BAT become crucially important to maintain body temperature when animals confront lower temperatures after a previous period of prolonged fasting.
source: However, these studies left open the question of the importance of endogenous BAT stores when animals confront lower temperatures after a previous period of prolonged fasting. Under such more stringent nutrient conditions, which we presume not to be uncommon in the wild, our findings indicate that energy reservoirs within BAT become crucially important to maintain body temperature.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mutant mice with depleted BAT energy stores cannot maintain body temperature during cold exposure after fasting.

claim: Abnormal catabolic function in BAT can compromise responses to cold exposure.
source: Our study indicates that abnormal catabolic function in BAT can indeed compromise responses to cold exposure.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mutant mice with increased BAT catabolism show impaired cold responses.

claim: Fasting induces expression of Klf15 in liver, where it upregulates gluconeogenesis.
source: Fasting induces expression of Klf15 in liver, where it upregulates gluconeogenesis, and in muscle, where it promotes amino acid degradation, thereby providing precursors for liver gluconeogenesis at the expense of muscle protein (Yamamoto et al., 2004; Gray et al., 2007; Shimizu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yamamoto et al., 2004, Gray et al., 2007, and Shimizu et al., 2011.

claim: Fasting induces expression of Klf15 in muscle, where it promotes amino acid degradation.
source: Fasting induces expression of Klf15 in liver, where it upregulates gluconeogenesis, and in muscle, where it promotes amino acid degradation, thereby providing precursors for liver gluconeogenesis at the expense of muscle protein (Yamamoto et al., 2004; Gray et al., 2007; Shimizu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yamamoto et al., 2004, Gray et al., 2007, and Shimizu et al., 2011.

claim: Glucocorticoid signaling appears to be responsible for Klf15 induction upon fasting in liver and muscle.
source: Glucocorticoid signaling appears to be responsible for Klf15 induction upon fasting in these tissues (Gray et al., 2007; Sasse et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gray et al., 2007 and Sasse et al., 2013.

claim: Klf15 expression was recently reported to be decreased in white adipocytes from fasted mice compared to fed mice.
source: In contrast, Klf15 expression was recently reported to be decreased in white adipocytes from fasted mice compared to fed mice (Matoba et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Matoba et al., 2017.

claim: WAT KLF15 inhibits lipolysis and promotes lipid storage in response to insulin, indicative of anabolic functions in this tissue.
source: The same study showed that WAT KLF15 inhibits lipolysis and promotes lipid storage in response to insulin, indicative of anabolic functions in this tissue.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Matoba et al., 2017 (implied from 'The same study').

claim: Muscle and BAT have been shown to originate from a common set of dermomyotome-derived precursor cells, which are distinct from those that give rise to WAT.
source: Interestingly, muscle and BAT have been shown to originate from a common set of dermomyotome-derived precursor cells, which are distinct from those that give rise to WAT (Wang and Seale, 2016), suggesting a possible reason for their sharing a similar mode of Klf15 regulation upon fasting.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang and Seale, 2016.

claim: The common developmental origin of muscle and BAT may explain their sharing a similar mode of Klf15 regulation upon fasting.
source: Interestingly, muscle and BAT have been shown to originate from a common set of dermomyotome-derived precursor cells, which are distinct from those that give rise to WAT (Wang and Seale, 2016), suggesting a possible reason for their sharing a similar mode of Klf15 regulation upon fasting.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on the observation that muscle and BAT share developmental origins and similar Klf15 regulation.

claim: A recent study investigated BAT-specific GR knock-out mice and concluded that glucocorticoid signaling is dispensable for control of energy homeostasis in BAT.
source: A recent study investigated BAT-specific GR knock-out mice and concluded that glucocorticoid signaling is dispensable for control of energy homeostasis in BAT (Glantschnig et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Glantschnig et al., 2019.

claim: POX can promote cell survival under conditions of limited nutrient availability through its ability to catabolize collagen-derived proline.
source: Previous studies in cancer cells have shown that POX can promote cell survival under conditions of limited nutrient availability through its ability to catabolize collagen-derived proline (Olivares et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Olivares et al., 2017.

claim: Proline is the most abundant amino acid in collagen.
source: Proline is the most abundant amino acid in collagen, itself a major component of the extracellular matrix of many tissues, including BAT.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Collagen is a major component of the extracellular matrix of many tissues, including BAT.
source: Proline is the most abundant amino acid in collagen, itself a major component of the extracellular matrix of many tissues, including BAT.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Under conditions of low fatty acid and glucose availability, increased POX expression in BAT lacking ALK7 may lead to channeling of TCA intermediates and mitochondrial generation of ATP.
source: Under conditions of low fatty acid and glucose availability, increased POX expression in BAT lacking ALK7 may lead to channeling of TCA intermediates and mitochondrial generation of ATP, as observed in fasted mutant mice, leaving these animals with fewer reserves to successfully confront exposure to cold temperatures.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on the observation that fasted mutant mice have increased POX and ATP generation.

claim: Upon cold exposure, BAT utilizes branched-chain amino acids for thermogenesis, promoting systemic clearance of these amino acids in both mice and humans.
source: In line with our findings, a recent study reported that, upon cold exposure, BAT utilizes branched-chain amino acids for thermogenesis, promoting systemic clearance of these amino acids in both in mice and humans (Yoneshiro et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yoneshiro et al., 2019.

claim: The mitochondrial enzyme BCAT2 is particularly important in the utilization of branched-chain amino acids for thermogenesis.
source: The mitochondrial enzyme BCAT2 was found to be particularly important in this process.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yoneshiro et al., 2019 (implied from context).

claim: Premature depletion of branched-chain amino acids under nutrient stress predisposes mutant mice lacking ALK7 in BAT to succumb to acute cold exposure.
source: Together, these observations suggest that premature depletion of branched-chain amino acids under nutrient stress predisposes mutant mice lacking ALK7 in BAT to succumb to acute cold exposure.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mutant mice have increased BCAT2 expression and show hypothermia during cold exposure after fasting.

claim: The role of ALK7 in mediating BAT responses to nutrient stress involves repression of the glucocorticoid/KL15/POX axis.
source: Our study reveals a novel mechanism for the role of ALK7 in mediating BAT responses to nutrient stress involving repression of the glucocorticoid/KL15/POX axis (Figure 6—figure supplement 5), which is distinct from the established role of ALK7 in regulating adrenergic activity in WAT during high caloric intake (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective observations of the study.

claim: The role of ALK7 in BAT is distinct from the established role of ALK7 in regulating adrenergic activity in WAT during high caloric intake.
source: Our study reveals a novel mechanism for the role of ALK7 in mediating BAT responses to nutrient stress involving repression of the glucocorticoid/KL15/POX axis (Figure 6—figure supplement 5), which is distinct from the established role of ALK7 in regulating adrenergic activity in WAT during high caloric intake (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2014 and comparison with current findings.

claim: Fasting is a well known stimulus of glucocorticoid release.
source: Fasting is a well known stimulus of glucocorticoid release (Dallman et al., 1993), and through the GR, glucocorticoids can stimulate transcription of the Klf15 gene in liver and muscle cells (Gray et al., 2007; Sasse et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dallman et al., 1993.

claim: Through the GR, glucocorticoids can stimulate transcription of the Klf15 gene in liver and muscle cells.
source: Fasting is a well known stimulus of glucocorticoid release (Dallman et al., 1993), and through the GR, glucocorticoids can stimulate transcription of the Klf15 gene in liver and muscle cells (Gray et al., 2007; Sasse et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gray et al., 2007 and Sasse et al., 2013.

claim: KLF15 increases expression of amino acid degrading enzymes POX, ALT1, BCAT2.
source: KLF15 in turn increases expression of amino acid degrading enzymes POX, ALT1, BCAT2 (Gray et al., 2007; Shimizu et al., 2011; Sasse et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gray et al., 2007, Shimizu et al., 2011, and Sasse et al., 2013.

claim: Activation of GR signaling by dexamethasone has been shown to increase expression of C/EBPα in hepatoma cells.
source: In addition, activation of GR signaling by dexamethasone has been shown to increase expression of C/EBPα in hepatoma cells (Cram et al., 1998) and the GR itself can interact directly with C/EBPα and increase its activity in different cell types (Rüdiger et al., 2002; Muratcioglu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cram et al., 1998.

claim: The GR can interact directly with C/EBPα and increase its activity in different cell types.
source: In addition, activation of GR signaling by dexamethasone has been shown to increase expression of C/EBPα in hepatoma cells (Cram et al., 1998) and the GR itself can interact directly with C/EBPα and increase its activity in different cell types (Rüdiger et al., 2002; Muratcioglu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rüdiger et al., 2002 and Muratcioglu et al., 2015.

claim: KLF15 can regulate C/EBPα expression in adipocytes.
source: It has also been demonstrated that KLF15 can regulate C/EBPα expression in adipocytes (Asada et al., 2011), establishing a further link between GR signaling and ATGL induction in these cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Asada et al., 2011.

claim: Loss of ALK7 leads to amplification of catabolic pathways, suggesting that ALK7 normally functions to suppress their activity.
source: Our results show that loss of ALK7 leads to amplification of these catabolic pathways, suggesting that ALK7 normally functions to suppress their activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that loss of ALK7 increases catabolic activity.

claim: ALK7 activation of Smad2/3 interferes with glucocorticoid signaling in adipocytes, either through direct binding of Smad proteins to the GR, or through intermediate proteins, such as transcriptional co-factors.
source: Although the detailed molecular mechanism remains to be clarified, our results suggest that ALK7 activation of Smad2/3, key mediators of signaling by TGF-β superfamily receptors, interferes with glucocorticoid signaling in adipocytes, either through direct binding of Smad proteins to the GR, or through intermediate proteins, such as transcriptional co-factors.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on the observation that ALK7 suppresses glucocorticoid-regulated pathways.

claim: Smad3 has been shown to interact directly with C/EBPβ and C/EBPδ, thereby inhibiting their ability to sustain C/EBPα expression in adipocytes.
source: In addition, Smad3 has been shown to interact directly with C/EBPβ and C/EBPδ, thereby inhibiting their ability to sustain C/EBPα expression in adipocytes (Choy and Derynck, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Choy and Derynck, 2003.

claim: The finding of increased levels of C/EBPα in iBAT of mutant mice after fasting is in agreement with the observation that Smad3 inhibits C/EBPα expression.
source: Our finding of increased levels of C/EBPα in iBAT of mutant mice after fasting is in agreement with this observation, and suggests another possible route for the effects of ALK7 on ATGL expression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that loss of ALK7 (and thus Smad signaling) leads to increased C/EBPα.

claim: Patients undergoing chronic (2 weeks) glucocorticoid treatment showed reduced BAT mass compared to controls.
source: We note that patients undergoing chronic (2 weeks) glucocorticoid treatment showed reduced BAT mass compared to controls (Ramage et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ramage et al., 2016.

claim: Chronic exposure to overactive glucocorticoid-regulated pathways in BAT of conditional mutant mice may exaggerate BAT catabolic functions, resulting in reduced BAT mass and lower thermogenic performance.
source: It is possible that chronic exposure to overactive glucocorticoid-regulated pathways in BAT of conditional mutant mice may exaggerate BAT catabolic functions, resulting in reduced BAT mass and lower thermogenic performance, even under normal feeding conditions.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on the observation that mutant mice show reduced BAT mass during chronic cold exposure.

claim: ALK7 functions by limiting nutrient stress-induced overactivation of catabolic activities in brown adipocytes.
source: We find that ALK7 functions by limiting nutrient stress-induced overactivation of catabolic activities in brown adipocytes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective observations of the study.

claim: ALK7 suppresses the levels of ATGL and amino acid degrading enzymes, including POX, through a novel pathway involving downstream effectors of glucocorticoid signaling, such as KLF15.
source: Mechanistically, it does so by suppressing the levels of ATGL, a key enzyme for lipolysis, and amino acid degrading enzymes, including POX, through a novel pathway involving downstream effectors of glucocorticoid signaling, such as KLF15, a master regulator of fasting responses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective observations of the study.

claim: ALK7 functions as a sensor to allow the brown adipocyte to adapt metabolically to the availability of nutrients.
source: Based on our results, we propose that ALK7 functions as a sensor to allow the brown adipocyte to adapt metabolically to the availability of nutrients.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective observations of the study.
